opus-5.5.text:
Around 2017, robotics was honestly a pretty unglamorous place to be. Deep learning had just had its big moments in vision and speech, and then AlphaGo, so the energy and the talent flowed toward problems where you could download a dataset, train on GPUs, and see results in days. Robotics wasn't like that at all.

First, the feedback loop was painfully slow. You couldn't just scrape the internet for robot data. Every data point came from a physical machine that breaks, drifts out of calibration, and needs someone standing next to it. A single experiment could take weeks, and a lot of that time was spent debugging hardware rather than doing research.

Second, the barrier to entry was high. You needed money for robots, lab space, and people who understood mechanical engineering, control theory, and machine learning at the same time. That's a rare combination, and most groups that had all of it were a handful of established labs.

Third, there wasn't a clear sense that learning would actually work for robots. The field was still dominated by classical methods: careful modeling, motion planning, hand-tuned controllers. Those work well in structured settings like factories, but they don't generalize. The learning-based approaches were promising in demos, but they were brittle, and many people looked at it and thought, this is a decade away, why spend my PhD on it?

And finally, the career incentives just weren't there. If you were a strong ML student, you could publish faster, get hired at a big tech company, and have more impact working on language or vision. Robotics felt like the hard road with an uncertain payoff.

So the people who stayed were the ones who really, stubbornly believed that intelligence has to be embodied, that it ultimately has to act in the physical world. It was a small community, but that's partly why it was so interesting. In hindsight, a lot of the groundwork people are building on now was laid by that small group during those quieter years.

r001.rationale: It says robotics required money for robots and lab space, identifying high hardware costs as a barrier.

r002.rationale: It says robotics required people who understood mechanical engineering, control theory, and machine learning, identifying specialized expertise as a barrier.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to a few things that were all true at the same time around 2017.

The first is that robotics just wasn't where the excitement was. That was the moment deep learning was exploding in vision, in speech, in language. If you were a bright PhD student and you wanted to publish fast and see your work actually get used, you went into those areas. In computer vision you could download a dataset, train a model overnight, and have a result by the morning. In robotics, you spent six months getting the hardware to work before you could even run your first real experiment.

And that's the second thing, the barrier to entry. Robotics is expensive and slow. You need a physical robot, which costs tens of thousands of dollars, it breaks, it needs a lab, it needs an engineer to maintain it. Most university groups could afford one or two arms, so maybe three or four students could do real experiments at any one time. You simply can't scale a research community when each data point requires a physical machine and a human standing next to it.

The third thing is that the field didn't have a clear scaling story yet. In language or vision, by 2017 people could already see the path: more data, more compute, better results. In robotics, data was scarce, every lab had a different robot, a different gripper, a different camera, so nothing transferred. There was no ImageNet for manipulation. Without that kind of shared benchmark, progress looked incremental and a lot of people concluded, maybe reasonably at the time, that it wasn't the right decade to bet on it.

And then there's the career incentive. Industry wasn't hiring robotics researchers the way it was hiring deep learning people. Google and Facebook were paying enormous salaries for anyone who could train a convnet. Robotics companies were mostly small and underfunded, and the big successes, like Boston Dynamics, were more about classical control than learning. So students looked at that and said, why would I spend five years on something with no obvious job at the end?

Looking back, I actually think that scarcity was healthy in a way. The people who stayed in robotics in 2017 were there because they genuinely cared about the problem, not because it was fashionable. A lot of the foundations that made the current wave possible, the simulation work, the early imitation learning, the hardware getting cheaper, got built quietly during those years by a relatively small group. It's only once large models made it clear that the same scaling recipe might apply to embodied intelligence that everyone suddenly rediscovered the field.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics was expensive and that a physical robot could cost tens of thousands of dollars.

r002.rationale: It says robots needed an engineer to maintain them, identifying specialized engineering expertise as a barrier to entering robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics was a difficult field to get into because you had to make so many things work together: hardware, control, perception, and planning. If an experiment failed, it wasn’t always clear whether the problem was your algorithm, a sensor, or the robot itself. That made research expensive and progress slow.

Around 2017, machine learning offered a much faster feedback loop. You could work with a dataset, train a model, and compare results without maintaining a physical system. So robotics attracted people, but the practical barriers meant fewer could actually do the research.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics research was expensive and ties the difficulty to experiments involving physical systems and robot hardware.

r002.rationale: It describes robotics as difficult to enter because researchers had to make hardware, control, perception, and planning work together, conveying the required breadth of expertise.

sol-6.1.text: I think robotics had a very high barrier to entry. Around 2017, if you wanted to do robotics research, you needed hardware, a lab, and expertise across several areas—mechanical engineering, control, perception, and software. You couldn’t just download a dataset and start experimenting on a laptop. Even a small experiment could involve a lot of setup and debugging, so progress was slow and expensive. That made it harder for people to enter the field and for small teams to produce results.

r001.rationale: It describes hardware and lab access as barriers and says robotics experiments were expensive, identifying hardware-related costs as a reason entry was difficult.

r002.rationale: It says robotics required expertise across mechanical engineering, control, perception, and software, making expert knowledge a barrier to entry.
